https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This informational letter is dated October 29, 2020, from Steve Coulter, School Products Manager at Hoekstra Transportation, to Rick West, Assistant Superintendent Business Services at the Troy School District, on the subject of fuel platforms available for school buses. Coulter recalls that last year Hoekstra provided a summary of fuel options offered through its manufacturer, Thomas Built Buses, and states that not much has changed since then. Hoekstra's view is that clean diesel remains the most affordable, sustainable, and efficient offering available. Current offerings include clean diesel, propane, CNG, and battery electric EV, and Hoekstra and Thomas Built Buses see clean diesel as the bridge to battery-electric school buses.

On battery electric, Coulter explains that the EV school bus must scale up to lower acquisition costs, and describes a pilot project to deliver the first EV school buses, the Thomas Built Jouley EV, to Ann Arbor and Roseville Schools. The project was directed by DTE, partnering with Thomas Built Buses and Proterra (the battery, traction drive, and charging station supplier), along with the dealership. Applications were submitted to EGLE, and each school was awarded grant funds through the Volkswagen Mitigation fund, which covered 70% of the cost of the bus, infrastructure, and charging stations; the total cost came to approximately $360,000 per bus. Coulter argues that without a grant the EV models are not yet ready for market, but that numerous pilot projects will build understanding of reliability and operating cost. He notes school bus operations are a good fit for EV because of limited miles and predictable returns to the terminal for recharging. Using an average of 15,000 miles annually at a fuel cost around $2.20 per gallon of diesel and 7.5 mpg conservatively, total fuel costs over a 12-year life cycle would be $52,800; the EV would operate for less, though the exact electricity cost is uncertain, and would have a lower cost of operation once it scales and battery costs decline. He predicts EV school buses will be a factor over the next decade.

On CNG (compressed natural gas), Coulter lists the highlights: a product upcharge of approximately $35,000; similar mpg to clean diesel; fuel that is approximately 40% less than clean diesel; and a fast-fill fueling station costing $1 to 1.5 million.

On propane, he lists a product upcharge of $8,000 to $10,000; fuel approximately 37% less money when including the federal 50-cent-per-gallon rebate available if fueling on site (subject to renewal each federal budget year); mpg approximately 34% less than clean diesel, requiring more fossil fuel for similar distances; and an engine that runs much hotter than diesel, with longevity being a question. The letter is a vendor-provided reference to inform the district's fuel and bus-purchasing decisions rather than a formal action item.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A press release, addressed to administrators, from the Michigan Council of Teachers of English (MCTE) diversity, inclusion, justice, and equity (dije) subcommittee, dated 08 October 2020 and included in the November 17, 2020 Regular Meeting of the Troy School District Board of Education. Written by Naitnaphit Limlamai, Chair of the dije subcommittee, the letter congratulates five Troy High School English teachers -- Jodie Duda, Erin Fischer-Ballew, Annie Gallagher, Christina Rick, and Valerie Valentino -- on receiving a dije professional-development grant in the Fall 2020 cycle.

The letter explains that the professional-development grant's goal is to support Michigan English teachers across the state as they engage in self-designed professional development that privileges diversity, inclusion, justice, and equity work. The five recipients created a program of reading and learning supporting their commitment to "disrupting stock stories, stereotypes, and westernized narratives." Their selected texts, described as demonstrating a desire to learn about themselves, their students, and pursuing justice and activism, are: Black Appetite. White Food: Issues of Race, Voice and Justice Within and Beyond the Classroom by Jamila Lyiscott; We Got This.: Equity, Access, and the Quest to Be Who Our Students Need Us to Be by Cornelius Minor (rendered "Miner" in the text); The Anti-Racist Teacher: Reading Instruction Workbook by Lorena German; Educating Activist Allies: Social Justice Pedagogy with the Suburban and Urban Elite by Katy Swalwell; and Linguistic Justice: Black Language, Literacy, Identity, and Pedagogy by April Baker-Bell. The teachers intend to use the concepts and practices from these readings to plan learning for their students, build community, and engage in "rich activist lives."

Limlamai expresses excitement to hear about what the teachers learn and how they engage their students and themselves in the work of activism. She notes that MCTE's annual conference had been postponed (a reference to pandemic-era disruptions) but looks forward to the teachers presenting their work to the community of Michigan English teachers and teacher educators when meetings resume, and to continuing to support their work as teachers and members of MCTE. The document serves as recognition of Troy High School staff accomplishment shared with the Board and public.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This is Board of Education business agenda item 12.C for the January 19, 2021 meeting, a Consideration and suggested resolution regarding the Section 1 Purchase Agreement Amendment for the sale of surplus district real property.

The resolution recites that the School District passed a resolution on April 21, 2020 authorizing the sale of surplus real property in the City of Troy, Oakland County, Michigan, described as 6.12 +/- acres of vacant land located on the north side of Square Lake Road, east of John R Road (the "Premises"). The Premises is part of a larger 70.647 +/- acre parcel (Parcel 2), and the District is additionally including an 11.281 +/- acre parcel (Parcel 1). The undeveloped portion of Parcel 2 and all of Parcel 1 are to remain preserved in perpetuity through a conservation easement.

In compliance with the approved resolution, the Superintendent negotiated and executed an offer to purchase dated June 8, 2020 (the "Purchase Agreement") with Robertson Brothers Co., on behalf of an entity to be formed (the "Purchaser"), to purchase the Premises for One Million Four Hundred Twenty Five Thousand Dollars ($1,425,000.00) (the "Purchase Price"), with an earnest money deposit of Fifty Thousand Dollars ($50,000.00).

The School District and Purchaser subsequently learned that up to an additional 6.29 acres of land is required to be deeded to the Purchaser in order to receive the necessary density bonus assumed in the Purchaser's Concept Plan under the City's One-Family Cluster Option Ordinance, which Concept Plan was incorporated by reference into the Purchase Agreement. An amendment to the Purchase Agreement is therefore required in order to deed, at closing, the additional acreage to the Purchaser; the amendment/deed will make clear that the additional acreage will remain preserved as open space in perpetuity, except for the storm pond/basin, the trailhead gravel parking lot, and other similar requirements necessary for the Purchaser's proposed development in accordance with its Concept Plan.

The operative resolution provides that: (1) the School District authorizes the Superintendent, or his designee, to negotiate an amendment to the current Purchase Agreement to include the additional acreage required to receive the density bonus under the City's One-Family Cluster Option Ordinance, adjust the timelines outlined in the Purchase Agreement accordingly, and agree to any other terms and conditions acceptable to the Superintendent after consultation with legal counsel, on terms substantially similar to those described; and (2) once satisfied with the negotiated amendment, the Superintendent or his designee is authorized to execute the amendment and any and all documents necessary and incidental to the sale of the Premises on behalf of the School District.

The resolution is decided by roll call vote, with members listed as Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt, Wilson, Anne, and Gottlieb, and includes a "Resolution Declared Adopted" line for the Secretary of the Board of Education. The certification language states that the foregoing is a true and complete copy of a resolution duly adopted by the Board of Education of the Troy School District, County of Oakland, Michigan, at a regular meeting held on January 19, 2021, conducted in full compliance with the Open Meetings Act (Act 267, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976). What it is
A Bond Formation Plan graphic/timeline for the Troy School District, mapping the phased process from initial planning to a successful bond election.

Phases and estimated durations
- Kickoff / Develop District Bond Plan (Discovery, ~2 weeks): engage administration, legal counsel, demographic and financial advisors; create bond formation schedule with key dates.
- Facilities & Program Definition (Exploration, ~2-4 months): tour all facilities to update and prioritize infrastructure needs; conduct technology, site/environmental, and enrollment audits; facilities assessment of all buildings; visioning sessions with key staff; review enrollment projections; identify deficiencies and upgrade opportunities.
- Concept Options Development (~1-2 months): develop concept options and estimated costs; present preliminary options for feedback; finalize concepts to test with the broader community.
- Community Engagement (~1-2 months): steering committee meetings (anticipate 4-6); professional market survey (4-6 weeks, $15K-$20K); community engagement sessions to educate members and test financial tolerance; possible district survey; analyze community responses.
- Bond Application (Pre-Qual, ~1 month): develop data for bond application; meet with the Department of Treasury; approve and submit final bond application.
- Bond Campaign (~3-6 months): district campaign leading to success at the polls.

Notes
Time durations often overlap. A bond steering committee is to be formed (by application or invitation) and presents its recommendation to the Board.

Purpose
Provides the visual roadmap and schedule for organizing a future bond program, supporting the related Bond Planning memo.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This document is the Troy School District Bond Formation Plan, presented as a phased graphic timeline that maps the steps from initial planning through a successful bond vote. It is an attachment supporting the district's bond planning discussion. The plan is organized into overlapping phases labeled Discovery, Exploration, Pre-Qual, and Campaign, with major stages: Kickoff / Develop District Bond Plan, Facilities & Program Definition, Concept Options Development, Community Engagement, Bond Application, and Bond Campaign / Vote. Estimated durations shown across the timeline range from 2 weeks to 3-6 months (2 weeks; 2-4 months; 1-2 months; 1-2 months; 1 month; 3 months; 3-6 months), and the plan notes that time durations often overlap.

In the Kickoff phase, the district would engage administration, legal counsel, and demographic and financial advisors to understand the financial and enrollment picture, and create a bond formation schedule with administration covering key dates and activities.

Under Facilities & Program Definition, activities include touring all facilities to update, document, and prioritize infrastructure needs; conducting other audits and reports as needed (technology; site and environmental; enrollment); conducting a facilities assessment of all district buildings; meeting with administration to discuss the program vision; conducting visioning sessions with key staff to understand and document program goals and facility needs; reviewing enrollment projections; comparing an ideal program of ingredients for each building level against existing buildings; and identifying deficiencies and opportunities for upgrades.

Under Concept Options Development, the plan calls for reviewing assessment data and program needs and merging ideas, developing concept options and estimated costs, presenting preliminary concept options for review and feedback, and finalizing concepts to test with the broader community.

Under Community Engagement, committee meetings begin (anticipating 4-6 meetings), including determining the appropriate method to seek community input, determining the composition of a Bond Steering Committee and the format for selecting members (application or invitation process), conducting a professional market survey (4-6 weeks, $15K-$20K), holding community engagement sessions to educate community members on assessment findings and to test concepts and financial tolerance, a possible district survey, analyzing community responses, and overlaying concepts with community feedback. The steering committee reviews community feedback and forms consensus on a recommendation, then presents that recommendation to the Board.

Under Bond Application (Pre-Qual), the district would develop data for the bond application, meet with the Department of Treasury, finalize program scope and cost, and approve and submit the final bond application. The final Bond Campaign phase involves a district campaign with strategy and communication tools aimed at success at the polls. The document overall serves as the visual roadmap and schedule for organizing a future Troy School District bond program.

A presentation and memorandum recommending Schools of Choice (SOC) program parameters for the Troy School District for the 2021-2022 school year, authored by Kris Griffor, Assistant Superintendent for Elementary Instruction, and Christine DiPilato, Assistant Superintendent for Secondary Instruction, in a memo dated February 2, 2021 to the TSD Board of Education.

Background on Schools of Choice notes it provides non-resident students additional enrollment opportunities, that participation is optional for districts, and that the degree of participation (application dates, grade levels, building assignments) is determined locally.

Enrollment projections were submitted by Plante Moran Cresa. "Most likely" versus actual figures include: Kindergarten 861 most likely / 849 actual (2018/2019), 835/838 (2019/2020), 844/761 as of 1/28/21 (2020/2021), and 845 projected for 2021/2022; First Grade 914/915, 891/888, 884/829 as of 1/28/21, and 851 projected for 2021/2022.

Elementary SOC application history from 2006-2007 through 2020-2021 totaled 1,035 kindergarten openings and 315 first-grade openings advertised, 1,959 and 580 applications received, and 1,060 and 268 students enrolled respectively.

For the 2020-2021 school year, elementary SOC students numbered 326 against 4,901 non-SOC students, a 6.24% SOC share (down 0.67%). By building: Barnard 42 (8.73%), Bemis 6 (1.19%), Costello 42 (10.32%), Hamilton 34 (7.34%), Hill 63 (18.64%), Leonard 36 (8.35%), Martell 21 (5.43%), Morse 7 (1.62%), Schroeder 1 (0.21%), Troy Union 16 (3.58%), TSD Preschool 0, Wass 44 (10.97%), and Wattles 14 (3.29%). By grade, SOC counts were Kindergarten 27, First 45, Second 43, Third 42, Fourth 80, and Fifth 89.

SOC demographic subgroups (elementary) included English Learners 53 (16.26%), Free/Reduced Lunch 60 (18.40%), and Special Education 25 (7.67%). By ethnicity, SOC students were 62.58% White (204), 21.47% Asian (70), 5.83% Black (19), 5.52% Multi-ethnic (18), 3.99% Hispanic (13), and 0.61% Hawaiian/Pacific Islander (2). District-wide non-SOC enrollment totaled 11,419 students across kindergarten through 12th grade.

A sibling-preference survey emailed to current SOC families identified siblings eligible for the 2021-2022 year: 10 kindergarten students, 1 first-grade student, and 9 middle-school students (grades 6-8 combined) planning to attend.

After considering current enrollment, projections, current SOC numbers and percentages, projected age-eligible siblings, and available elementary classrooms, the recommendation was to use Plante Moran Cresa projection numbers as the foundation and to accept SOC applications for 50 Kindergarten, 50 First Grade, and 20 Middle School students for the 2021-2022 school year.

Project description: The week's Board packet includes a project for districtwide UPS (uninterruptible power supply) replacement. UPS units are battery backups that keep power on to the district's main network closets so that phones in the office will continue working in the event of a power outage for at least 20 minutes. A UPS unit also provides protection for equipment in the event of power spikes, brownouts, or other electrical abnormalities. Under this project, the district will replace the UPS units at all buildings except the Preschool, TLC, and Services.

E-rate eligibility: This is an E-rate eligible project and will be reimbursed at 40 percent for all units except those being installed at Rankin, Central Office, and Transportation. Buildings that do not house students are not E-rate eligible.

Vendor rationale: The recommendation letter in the packet explains the rationale for vendor selection. By selecting Capricorn, the district gets a UPS with a 10-year life and warranty. Units proposed by other vendors would need replacement again in 5 years due to the nature of their proposed sealed lead-acid batteries. For less than $2,000, the district gains an extra 5 years of useful life because the Capricorn product carries a 10-year warranty and utilizes lithium-ion batteries.

Funding: This is a project budgeted in the Bond, and aside from three units (those at Rankin, Central Office, and Transportation), all equipment is eligible for 40 percent reimbursement through E-rate. Memorandum dated January 27, 2021, on Technology Services letterhead (4420 Livernois; Phone 248.823.5060), from Beth Soggs, Director of Technology, to Rick West, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, regarding the Fiber Maintenance Agreement for Troy School District.

E-rate framework: E-rate requires the district to bid out fiber maintenance every three years for district-owned fiber, ensuring eligibility for 40% reimbursement on all maintenance and repair expenses on district-owned fiber. E-rate requires an annual MAXIMUM estimate from bidders, and any amount spent over the awarded vendor's estimated maximum is not eligible for reimbursement. Soggs stresses that the dollar amount is only a maximum estimate and the district pays only for actual hours and materials used. Some years require little maintenance; others bring ice storms, I-75 Modernization projects, new construction, and DTE pole audits.

Evaluation: Soggs notes that the numbers estimated by responding vendors vary greatly, but the vendor that appears extremely high is actually the lowest cost and has a maximum estimate that exceeds current annual expenditures, ensuring every dollar spent is eligible for reimbursement. The proposals were thoroughly evaluated, and FiberLink has the lowest rates on every aspect aside from the fee charged to respond to a MissDig ticket and the optional fiber ride out. The past two years had an excessive number of MissDig tickets due to the I-75 road work and related surface street updates; now that this project has moved beyond Troy, MissDig tickets are anticipated to return to much lower historical levels. The ride out is an optional service the district does not plan to utilize at this time.

Additional rationale: Beyond the lowest labor rates, FiberLink is closest geographically to Troy, providing quicker response times and fewer travel hours charged. FiberLink has a long-standing relationship with the district, has provided excellent service and response times, and knows the district's fiber routes often without consulting maps. Soggs recommends FiberLink for the three-year agreement based on lowest cost per hour rates, proximity to the district, the maximum estimate that ensures every dollar is eligible for reimbursement, and the long-standing relationship.

Cost comparison method: The recommendation letter and supporting documentation include a cost comparison of the three vendors, built by taking the labor hours incurred on the 4 major repair projects since July and applying each vendor's hourly rates. FiberLink is significantly less; these 4 projects alone would have met or exceeded the E-rate maximum for the other two responding vendors, meaning work for the remaining 6 months would not have been eligible for 40% reimbursement had a vendor other than FiberLink been selected.

Funding: This is an E-rate eligible project, and all work except new builds (none planned) is eligible for 40% reimbursement. It is an annually budgeted General Fund expenditure.

Present via Zoom (all connecting from Troy, Michigan) were Board members Schmidt, Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, and Wilson. Also present were Superintendent Dr. Richard Machesky; administrators Birmingham, Carrier, Griffor, DiPilato, Moynihan, Carson, Zawislak, Harris, and West; attorney Dana Abrahams of Clark Hill, P.C.; two Student Board Representatives; and approximately 275 additional audience members.

Student Representative reports opened the meeting so students could prepare for mid-terms. Nathania Nartey (Athens High School) and Pranay Gupta (International Academy-East) shared updates; Sejal Patil (Troy High School) and Carlton Thomas (Troy College & Career High School) were not in attendance.

Schmidt explained the evening's meeting elects officers, appoints committee members for the upcoming year, and approves items requiring annual consideration, with the regular meeting to follow.

Actions taken (with resolution numbers and votes):
- Election of Acting Chairperson (21-002): Moved by Philippart, supported by Wilson, that Schmidt serve as acting chairperson until a president is elected. Roll call 7-0 (Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt, Wilson, Anne, Gottlieb all Yes).
- Appointment of Temporary Secretary: Schmidt appointed Judy Holmes to act until the Board secretary is elected.
- Nomination and Election of President (21-003): Hauff nominated Schmidt. Nominations closed 7-0. Moved by Hauff, supported by Anne, RESOLVED that Schmidt serve as president until December 31, 2021. Roll call vote 6 Yes (Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt, Wilson, Anne, Gottlieb) to 1 No (Hammond).
- Nomination and Election of Vice President (21-004): Philippart nominated Wilson. Nominations closed 7-0. Moved by Philippart, supported by Anne, RESOLVED that Wilson serve as vice president until December 31, 2021. Roll call 7-0.
- Nomination and Election of Secretary (21-005): Hammond nominated Hauff. Nominations closed 7-0. Moved by Hammond, supported by Philippart, RESOLVED that Hauff serve as secretary until December 31, 2021. Roll call 7-0.
- Appointment of School Board Treasurer (21-006): Moved by Philippart, supported by Anne, RESOLVED that Rick L. West, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, be appointed Treasurer of the Troy Board of Education for January through December 2021. Roll call 7-0.
- Establish Fund Depositories and Investments (21-007): A motion by Philippart, supported by Hammond, was underway (the minutes text is truncated at this point).

The minutes document the district's annual organizational governance for 2021, memorializing the officer slate (Schmidt/Wilson/Hauff) and the treasurer appointment, all with terms running through December 31, 2021.
